records.name: Benin
records.summary: Benin is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but 76crimes documents that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace; the Hirondelles Club provides safe housing for LGBT youth fleeing family violence. No LGR, no anti-discrimination law; community organises underground.

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2024): interview with Luc Agblakou, founder of the Hirondelles Club in Benin, which since 2013 has supported LGBT+ people with housing - founded after a father murdered his gay son. Nearly 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed through its 20-place temporary accommodation centre; the organisation now has branches in Togo, Burkina Faso and Niger. Article notes anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations are not criminalised in Benin, but there is no SOGISC discrimination protection, no legal gender recognition, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. LGBTIQ people face stigma from the public and police, which cracked down on a 'network of homosexuals' in 2022. The 2021 Benin Human Rights Commission report flagged physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention, torture and degrading treatment against LGBTQI+ people; LBQ women rarely report violence to police.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Benin: official assessment including the section on acts of violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity - same-sex conduct not criminalised but no protections; documents societal stigma and police treatment.
Washington Blade (Aug 2015): 'Voices from LGBT Catholics in Western Africa' — faithful in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria describe persecution and discrimination within the church and society.

Erasing 76 Crimes (May 2012): interview with anthropologist Patrick Awondo - homosexuality has a long history in Africa (evidence in Cameroon, Zimbabwe, Burkina Faso and Benin, including Mossi kings' relations with pages and marriages between women in Dahomey); colonial-era laws and anti-discrimination activism are the Western imports.

freshness.fact: Adult same-sex acts legal; art.545 (2018 code) adds penalties for acts with minors; strong social hostility and lynchings; 2023 US State picture holds.

records.name: Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba)
records.summary:
These are not autonomous countries but special municipalities of the kingdom itself, so metropolitan equality law applies directly: same-sex marriage has been performed on the islands since 2012 — one small island hosted the region's first such wedding after the 2010 status change and markets civil ceremonies openly — with the state's penal-code discrimination grounds and partnership frameworks in force, and a current-status review confirming no later change.

The caveats are the kingdom's own, and they are real: legal gender change still requires a medical expert's statement (the self-declaration act was withdrawn at kingdom level in July 2025), non-binary markers demand months-long court procedure, and three tiny church-dense communities leave service depth thin — the same rights overview that documents these gaps rates them with the metropolitan standard attached. Travel-side evidence is warm and wedding-positive; no adverse enforcement is documented.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview for the Netherlands (updated March 2026): progressive laws with gaps - legal gender change still requires a medical expert letter; nonbinary 'X' marker only via a 3-9 month court procedure; the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025. Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba) follows Dutch law as special municipalities.
GayCities (Dec 2022): top 10 Caribbean/Latin American destinations celebrating marriage equality - travel-oriented overview for same-sex couples planning destination weddings.

Dutch Caribbean Legal Portal (Dec 2012): the first same-sex wedding in Caribbean Netherlands, performed on Saba for two visiting residents - Saba was the first island of the former Netherlands Antilles to facilitate same-sex weddings after the 2010 constitutional status change.

Saba Tourism official weddings page: markets the island for destination weddings (civil ceremonies at the Court Room, flexible registrar) - relevant as Saba performs same-sex marriages under Dutch law.

freshness.fact: Dutch equality law applies to the public bodies; same-sex marriage performed on Bonaire/Sint Eustatius/Saba since 2018; no later change found.

records.name: Burkina Faso
records.summary:
Burkina Faso is dangerous for trans visitors. In July 2024 the military junta approved a revised Personal and Family Code criminalising homosexuality — Burkina Faso had never previously outlawed it. The junta (Traoré) has clamped down on opposition and media, promised elections have not been held, and much of the country faces jihadist insurgency. Enforcement details of the new law remain unclear (HDT notes drafting uncertainty), but the direction and the absence of any institutional recourse are unambiguous.

For a visitor: new criminalisation under a junta, plus severe general security conditions.

sources.claim: BBC (July 2024): Burkina Faso's military junta approved legislation to ban homosexual acts - previously not outlawed though socially frowned upon. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala announced the cabinet approval as part of a marriage-law overhaul that recognises only religious and customary marriages; the law still needed passage by the military-controlled parliament and junta leader Traoré's signature.

Africanews (July 2024): the junta approved revised marriage-family legislation criminalising homosexuality with 'severe penalties', as part of the same overhaul recognising only religious and customary marriages. (Article body largely behind page furniture at fetch time.)

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Burkina Faso: pre-criminalisation baseline - no law criminalising same-sex conduct; documents security-force abuses, prison conditions and societal discrimination (no LGBT-specific section content in the retrieved text).
HRW (Sept 2025): Burkina Faso criminalises same-sex conduct - the junta's law took effect, with prison sentences; HRW's reporting on the new penal provisions.
CNN (Sep 2025): 'Burkina Faso parliament passes law outlawing LGBTQ practices' — a new criminal-code article punishes 'LGBTQ practices' with up to five years.

LGBTQ Nation (Sept 2025): Burkina Faso's junta unanimously passed a law banning homosexuality - 2-5 years' imprisonment plus fines, per Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala; foreigners will be deported under the law; the country had never previously banned homosexuality.

freshness.fact: New criminal code in force 1 Sep 2025 criminalises same-sex acts and 'promotion' of homosexuality (junta bill of Jul 2024) — previously legal. Sharply worse.

records.name: Bangladesh
records.summary:
Bangladesh is a dangerous destination for trans visitors, with escalating Islamist violence since the August 2024 political crisis that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in February 2025 (police suspect extremist involvement). A human-rights group documented 260 anti-LGBTQI+ incidents in 2024 — including murder, arson, and blackmail — describing attacks as having "skyrocketed." Islamist fundamentalist groups have intensified attacks under the interim government, and LGBTQ+ people have been "forced into hiding." A mob stormed the gate of a safe house for third-gender people (one survivor said "I escaped only with my life").

Police extort hijra/trans people — dozens were arrested for refusing to pay extortion money, and five were arrested at Dhaka's international airport.

The US State Department rates Bangladesh as Level 3 (Reconsider Travel).

sources.claim: Erasing 76 Crimes (Feb 2025): prominent trans activist Shila was brutally murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025; police suspect extremists due to the nature of the attack. She was known for advocating legal recognition, healthcare access and safe spaces. JusticeMakers Bangladesh in France (JMBF) condemned the murder and called for legal reform.

Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2026): JMBF's annual report on 2025 documented 260 incidents of human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals in Bangladesh - a sharp increase continuing an upward trend since 2022 - including murder, arson and blackmail, with the interim government failing to protect them. Section 377 criminalises same-sex relations; the 2013 hijra recognition policy has not translated into effective protection or equal access to employment, healthcare, justice or services.

Global Press Journal feature: after the 2024 Monsoon Revolution, rising conservative Islamist influence has upended trans and third-gender lives in Dhaka - a mob stormed a third-gender safe house, community leaders went into hiding, and trans people are retreating from public life and erasing identities they once displayed openly. Notes third-gender recognition since 2013 and a trans woman elected mayor of a rural town in 2021.
Washington Blade (Aug 2025): 'LGBTQ Bangladeshis increasingly vulnerable a year after government toppled' — threats and attacks rise amid Islamist mobilisation and collapsing protections.

UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Bangladesh (updated April 2026): official UK asylum guidance assessing the legal position (Section 377), the hijra third-gender recognition, societal treatment, state protection levels, and risk to LGBT individuals - detailed country-of-origin information.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the 1860 Penal Code outlaws 'intercourse against the order of nature' with up to life imprisonment; rarely enforced but used by police as a pretext to harass perceived LGBTIQ people. Hijra people have been legally recognised as a third gender since 2014. Islamist groups have become vocal opponents - a BRAC University professor publicly tore a school textbook containing a transgender character, sparking backlash against gender diversity.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Oct 2025): dozens of hijras arbitrarily arrested across Bangladesh after refusing to pay extortion money to police, per JMBF. In Chattogram, at least twelve hijras were injured in an assault after filing a police complaint; in Narayanganj, twelve hijras were arrested while collecting money from vehicles - a traditional livelihood. JMBF alleges false extortion cases.

Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2024): five trans/hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to one month by a mobile court for 'extortion' and 'public disturbance'. JMBF condemned the convictions as exacerbating marginalisation of an already vulnerable group.

UK Upper Tribunal (Immigration and Asylum Chamber) decision PA/07096/2017 (Feb 2019): a Bangladeshi gay man's asylum appeal - the Home Office accepted Section 377 criminalises same-sex activity but argued it is not fully enforced; the decision examines country evidence on risk to gay men in Bangladesh - detailed case-law assessment of the actual risk profile.

freshness.fact: Section 377 ambiguity persists (life imprisonment for 'unnatural offences'); hijra third gender since 2014; five men caned Apr 2026 — enforcement continues.

records.name: Bulgaria
records.summary:
Bulgaria is workable for trans visitors — an EU member with no traveler-facing restrictions, but one of the EU's most hostile social climates. There is no bathroom law, no border friction for foreign passports, and no criminalisation of gender expression. The European Court of Justice is actively hearing the Shipov case on Bulgaria's refusal to issue ID matching lived gender, and EU free-movement law provides a legal backstop.

The concerns are climate rather than traveler law: the Supreme Court of Cassation ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible (gender an "unchangeable biological factor"), parliament passed a Russia-style law banning "propaganda" of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools (August 2024), and the EU's FRA survey finds 75% of LGBTIQ people in Bulgaria avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault — both far above EU averages. Hate speech by politicians is routine.

For a visitor: document mismatch carries no legal penalty, police do not target trans expression, and Sofia has a small but visible scene. The risk is street hostility if read as trans — verbal harassment is common, physical assault possible but not systematic.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Bulgaria: in August 2024 a law banning representation of LGBTI identities in schools was introduced (spearheaded by Vazrazhdane leader Kostadinov); Bulgaria continues rejecting asylum requests by LGBTI people from Russia and Belarus and unlawfully detains LGBTI asylum-seekers from Palestine in closed detention; a Sofia Pride performer received death threats; a LGBTI youth organisation faced institutional checks.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations decriminalised in 1968; anti-discrimination laws since 2004, expanded in 2015 to cover 'sex change' under 'sex'. But Article 46 of the constitution bans same-sex marriage, and there is no legal gender recognition. Koilova and Babulkova v. Bulgaria (ECtHR 2023) found Bulgaria in violation of its obligations on non-recognition of same-sex relationships.

EU FRA LGBTIQ survey III country sheet for Bulgaria (2024): 75% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (EU-27: 53%); 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault (EU-27: 29%); only 27% are open about being LGBTIQ (EU-27: 51%); 28% felt discriminated against at work or looking for work. Indicates a strongly hostile day-to-day climate.

DW (Sept 2025): ECJ Advocate General Richard de la Tour issued a non-binding opinion that Bulgaria must not refuse a trans woman ID documents matching her presented sex ('lived gender identity') - the Shipov case, concerning a Bulgarian trans woman on hormone therapy refused documents; such opinions are followed by the Court in roughly two-thirds of cases.

Strasbourg Observers analysis (Dec 2024) of Y.T. v. Bulgaria: the original 2020 ECtHR judgment found an Article 8 violation over refusal of legal gender recognition; on revision (July 2024) the application was declared inadmissible for abuse of rights, but the Court confirmed Bulgaria remains obliged under Article 8 (per P.H. v. Bulgaria) to provide a framework for legal gender recognition - which Bulgaria still lacks.

Amnesty International report (Feb 2015): 'Missing the point' - Bulgaria's failure to adequately investigate and prosecute hate crimes fuels fear, discrimination and violence against asylum seekers, migrants, Muslims and LGBT people; authorities consistently fail to identify bias motivation.
Human Rights Watch (Jun 2017): 'Sofia LGBT Pride Should Showcase a Tolerant Bulgaria' — op-ed urging authorities to protect Sofia Pride and show a tolerant face.
Novinite (June 2011): the 4th Sofia Pride passed without incidents under heavy police guard - after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 parades; only a 'family NGO' protested.

records.name: Bahrain
records.summary:
Bahrain is a place to avoid entirely, but with the thinnest active-enforcement record in the Gulf. Uniquely among Gulf states, same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1976, and there is no statute criminalising transgender expression. The UK foreign office notes "arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare."

However, broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions are used against gender and sexual minorities — penalties include imprisonment, fines, and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a Manama hotel discotheque on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. A Brazilian trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite a female passport marker. In 2023 a court rejected a trans man's recognition application citing Islamic Sharia, and in February 2024 the lower house of parliament adopted a bill to criminalise "acts of deviance" — a deteriorating trajectory.

For a visitor: the legal exposure is real but enforcement is sporadic; the modal risk is indecency arrest followed by deportation rather than imprisonment.

sources.claim: Wikipedia overview: same-sex sexual activity decriminalised in Bahrain since 1976; gender identity recognition 'limited'; no discrimination protections, no relationship recognition, no LGBT-inclusive family rights. Sections cover enforcement incidents, false accusations, and derogatory terminology.

Cairo 52 analysis (Feb 2024): in May 2023 a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia - despite extensive medical documentation from Bahrain and abroad. The court cited Sharia to deny both healthcare and recognition.

Cairo 52 country review of Bahrain: independent human-rights researchers and advocates (including UN bodies and Amnesty) have long been denied entry or research access, so local media are the main source on trans arrests and legal details are scarce. Laws are used to punish gender non-conformity; discriminatory violence by state and non-state actors is widely reported; trans people are denied gender-affirming healthcare (intersex people are permitted medical transition).

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Bahrain decriminalised same-sex relations in 1976 and is the only Gulf state not explicitly penalising same-sex intimacy - but authorities use 'indecency'/'debauchery' provisions to arrest queer and trans people. A February 2024 bill criminalising 'acts of deviance' with a person of the same sex and its 'promotion' had not passed into law as of March 2026. No LGBTIQ organisations operate; a 2023 court denied a trans man's gender-marker change, echoing a 2016 ruling.

Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, Response to Information Request BHR105575.E (2016): 'Bahrain: Situation of sexual minorities, including societal attitudes and treatment by authorities (2011–July 2016)'.

Pride Source (Jan 2010): 'Cross-dressers arrested in Bahrain' — nine cross-dressers of various Arab nationalities arrested at a Manama hotel discotheque on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery.

English translation of Bahrain's Penal Code 1976 (MENA Rights Group): the full criminal code text - includes the morality provisions (Articles 324-325 'outraging public decency' and related offences) used against gender-nonconforming people, though same-sex conduct itself is not explicitly criminalised.

freshness.fact: Consensual same-sex conduct not criminalised (2023 US State); courts since 2023 reject gender-affirming procedures; legal gender recognition still denied.

records.name: Bahamas
records.summary: The Bahamas demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 1991; tourism-dependent economy with extensive international exposure; no LGR; documented social hostility but no criminalisation and no police-targeting pattern.

sources.claim: ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for the Bahamas: documents the legal status of same-sex conduct (decriminalised by the 1991 sexual-offences law, with a higher same-sex age of consent) and gender recognition.

The Tribune (April 2016): 'Transgender plea for rights' - Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United (BTIU) launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign calling for equal access to healthcare, education and employment without discrimination, during the gender-equality referendum debate; spokesperson Alexus D'Marco described the constraints of socially accepted behaviour in The Bahamas.

GayLawNet Bahamas laws page: consensual same-sex sex lawful at 18 (Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act 1991, with life imprisonment for sex with a same-sex minor); in 1998 the National Security Minister stated the military, prison service and police do not discriminate based on sexual orientation.

The Tribune (May 2017): an American visitor was beaten at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, alleging he was 'targeted and beat up' because he is gay; he sought hate-crime charges and planned to sue - documents violence against an LGBT visitor.

freshness.fact: Male acts decriminalised 1991, no recent legal change; social homophobia prominent (Dec 2018 Canadian travel advice) — still the tourist climate.

records.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
records.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; Sarajevo Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 with heavy (necessary) police protection; and most cantons have now appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes — genuine institutional progress. Counterweights from the 2024 Pink Report: negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside Sarajevo (especially Republika Srpska), and trans people occupy a “precarious position” — no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to Sarajevo and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in Republika Srpska and rural areas.

sources.claim: Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024 (annual report on the human rights of LGBT persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina): the position of LGBTI people is unsatisfactory nationwide with a growing disparity between the two entities. In Republika Srpska there was an organised hooligan attack on BH Pride March activists in Banja Luka, incitement to violence and discrimination by the entity's highest officials, and organised anti-LGBT groups.

Balkan Diskurs feature (Oct 2024): legal gender recognition is formally accessible across BiH but described as vague and ineffective in practice - legal texts imply it requires complete medical transition, contradicting self-determination (criticised by the European Parliament). Without documents matching appearance, trans people face difficulties accessing housing and jobs; medical transition becomes a prerequisite for basic rights.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on BiH: eight SOGIESC hate-speech cases documented ahead of Sarajevo Pride; prosecutor offices in the majority of cantons now have staff overseeing anti-LGBTI hate crimes; the Federal Government instructed the Justice Ministry to draft a same-sex partnership law; the first Constitutional Court appeal was filed over non-recognition of a Croatian-issued same-sex partnership; extremists roamed Banja Luka chanting 'kill the...' before Pride events.
Human Rights Watch (Feb 2014): 'Bosnia and Herzegovina: Attack on LGBT Activists' — condemns a violent attack on Sarajevo Pride organisers; impunity and hate-motive failures documented.

GlobalGayz report (2012): 'Gay Life in Bosnia and Herzegovina' - decriminalised in FBiH (1996) and RS (1998); the 2009 anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation/sexual expression but omitted gender identity; describes a homophobic society across the two entities.

Sarajevo Open Centre (July 2016): BiH's amended Anti-discrimination Law explicitly covers sexual orientation and gender identity (with correct local terminology) and 'sex characteristics' - the first country in South-East Europe to protect intersex people in all spheres; also improves harassment definitions and procedures.

Sarajevo Open Centre (July 2016): the Federation of BiH adopted hate-crime regulation covering sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances - all three BiH administrative units now regulate hate crimes in their criminal codes.

freshness.fact: Legal state-wide (1996/98/2003); entities restrict marriage to opposite-sex couples; uneven protections, 2023 activist attack; ILGA-2024 picture stands.

evidence.title: LGBTQ rights in Bosnia and Herzegovina
